profile.feeling: Little salty-sour buds from a thorny bush that hangs from old walls — pickled, they wake up a sauce.

senses.def: caper — the bush (Capparis spinosa) and its pickled flower buds (mass noun)

examples.tr: Add the capers to the tomato sauce.

examples.text: يَنْمُو الْكَبَرُ بَيْنَ حِجَارَةِ الْجُدْرَانِ الْقَدِيمَةِ.
examples.tr: The caper bush grows between the stones of old walls.
I bought a jar of pickled capers.

synonyms.nuance: alternative form with the Syriac q and a long ā; also قُبَّار (Wiktionary)
alternative form with a long ā (Wiktionary)
old name of the caper, listed in Wiktionary’s translation table

etymology.text: From Classical Syriac ܩܦܪ (qappar, “caper bush”) or ܟܦܪ (kappar), considered to come from Ancient Greek κάππαρις (kápparis), of uncertain, probably Asian origin (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Greek κάππαρη, Turkish kapari, German Kaper, Russian каперсы and English caper all go back to Greek κάππαρις, like Arabic كَبَر.
pitfalls: Only the vowels separate كَبَر (kabar, capers) from كِبَر (kibar, old age), كِبْر (kibr, pride) and the verb كَبُرَ (kabura, to grow up) (Wiktionary).
subtleties: A mass noun: one bud = حَبَّةُ كَبَرٍ.
The word names both the bush and the buds; the context (a jar, a sauce, a wall) decides.

profile.feeling: A long, pale, ribbed “cucumber” that is really a melon — crisp summer food, and a word straight out of the Qurʾān.

senses.def: Armenian cucumber, snake melon (Cucumis melo var. flexuosus); collective — one fruit = قِثَّاءَة
cucumbers and melons in general, the genus Cucumis (Wiktionary)

examples.text: الْقِثَّاءُ أَطْوَلُ مِنَ الْخِيَارِ وَأَفْتَحُ لَوْنًا.
examples.tr: Armenian cucumbers are longer than cucumbers and lighter in colour.
I bought a long Armenian cucumber.
We eat Armenian cucumber raw with salt.

examples.text: رَأَيْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَأْكُلُ الرُّطَبَ بِالْقِثَّاءِ.
examples.tr: I saw the Messenger of God eat fresh dates with snake melon.

phrases.text: مِنْ بَقْلِهَا وَقِثَّائِهَا وَفُومِهَا وَعَدَسِهَا وَبَصَلِهَا
phrases.tr: of its herbs and its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils and its onions
phrases.meaning: The Children of Israel ask Moses for the vegetables of Egypt instead of manna — قِثَّاء is among them.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday name in Egypt and the Levant (Wiktionary: Armenian cucumber; one fruit فَقُّوسَة)

etymology.text: Proto-Semitic according to Kogan and Aro: cognate with Akkadian qiššû and Ge’ez ቍሳይ (“cucumber”), Hebrew קשוא (“Armenian cucumber”) and Syriac qaṭṭūtā; a wanderword also seen in Sumerian ukuš, Greek σίκυος and Latin cucumis. Doublet of كُوسَا (“zucchini”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Israelites’ longing for Egypt’s food is told twice: Numbers 11:5 lists הַקִּשֻּׁאִים, Qurʾān 2:61 lists قِثَّاء — the same word.
Modern Hebrew קִשּׁוּא (kishu) now means zucchini, and Arabic كُوسَا (zucchini, node veg.1) is a doublet of قِثَّاء (Wiktionary).
pitfalls: Botanically a melon (Cucumis melo), not a cucumber (Cucumis sativus = خِيَار).
Two vocalizations are correct: قِثَّاء and قُثَّاء (Wiktionary).
subtleties: Collective: الْقِثَّاءُ (the vegetable), قِثَّاءَة (one fruit), قِثَّاءَات (counted fruits).
The final hamza is part of the root, so the word is triptote: قِثَّاءٌ, قِثَّاءً — unlike diptotes such as هِنْدِبَاءُ.

profile.feeling: A cone-shaped, tender, sweet spring cabbage.

examples.text: الْمَلْفُوفُ الْمَخْرُوطِيُّ أَطْرَى مِنَ الْمَلْفُوفِ الْعَادِيِّ.
examples.tr: Pointed cabbage is more tender than ordinary cabbage.
I shredded the pointed cabbage for the salad.
I bought a head of pointed cabbage.

profile.synonymsNone: No other name; Wiktionary gives only مَلْفُوف مَخْرُوطِيّ, a description.

etymology.text: مَلْفُوف “cabbage”, from the passive participle of لَفَّ (“to wrap”), + مَخْرُوطِيّ “conical”, from مَخْرُوط (“cone”) + ـِيّ; Wiktionary gives the phrase as the translation of pointed cabbage.
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): ملفوف, مخروطي and the translation table of English pointed cabbage

funFacts: German Spitzkohl (“pointed cabbage”) draws the same picture; Wiktionary compares مَخْرُوط (cone) with Hebrew חָרוּט (kharut, “cone”).
pitfalls: The adjective agrees in case and definiteness: الْمَلْفُوفُ الْمَخْرُوطِيُّ, مَلْفُوفًا مَخْرُوطِيًّا — not *الْمَلْفُوفُ مَخْرُوطِيٌّ, which would be a sentence (“the cabbage is conical”).
subtleties: مَخْرُوطِيّ is the ordinary geometry word: شَكْلٌ مَخْرُوطِيٌّ, “a conical shape” — the name is a plain description, not a fixed brand of cabbage.
